name: XGBoost with SHAP explanations on the lake-year table

identity.method_name: XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin 2016) gradient-boosted trees with TreeSHAP (Lundberg et al. 2018/2020) explanations
identity.core_idea: Gradient boosting fits a sequence of shallow decision trees, each one trained to correct the residual error of the trees before it, to predict a target (e.g. water-area fraction, an encroachment index, or year-over-year change) from the project's tabular features (water/vegetation/built-up fractions, OSM building and road counts, rainfall, lake identity, year). TreeSHAP then decomposes each individual prediction into additive per-feature contributions using the exact tree structure, in principle giving both a global feature-importance ranking and a local, per-row explanation. This is the 'guide-friendly' tabular model because it produces plots (SHAP summary/beeswarm, dependence plots) that read as rigorous, interpretable machine learning to a non-specialist panel.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. Operates on the project's own 42-row lake-year table, which is not an official or externally published dataset; the model itself (xgboost.XGBClassifier / XGBRegressor) and explainer (shap.TreeExplainer) are open-source software packages, not datasets.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Whatever proxy target the 42-row table already uses (most likely a continuous water/vegetation/built-up area or an MNDWI-derived encroachment index computed by the project's own classical method) becomes XGBoost's regression or classification target. This is a threshold-rule proxy, not an independent label: the model is being asked to predict a number that was itself derived from MNDWI/NDVI thresholds on the same imagery whose other-derived features (vegetation fraction, water fraction) are also inputs. That circularity is a serious, separate risk from the sample-size problem addressed below, and should be disclosed regardless of what is decided about sample size.
fit_to_project.input_required: The existing 42-row x N-column lake-year table (lake ID, year, water/vegetation/built-up area or fraction, OSM building count, OSM road count/length, rainfall, and any other engineered features). All of this is already available in the project; no new acquisition is needed for the model to run, but see viable_with_42_rows for why running it is not the same as it being defensible.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: no, in any statistically honest sense, and this must be stated plainly rather than softened. XGBoost, like all gradient boosting implementations, fits trees by repeatedly splitting on whichever feature and threshold most reduces training loss at each step; with only 42 rows, a tree of even modest depth (3-4 splits) can partition the data into leaves containing a handful of rows each, meaning the model can trivially memorise which of the 6 lakes (or even which specific lake-year) it is looking at rather than learning a generalisable water/vegetation/built-up relationship. The effective number of independent statistical units is 6 (the number of clusters/lakes), not 42, because the 7 yearly observations within a lake are not independent of each other (they share the same static geometry, the same OSM footprint data, and largely the same local hydrology). Six independent units is far below any published guideline for tree-ensemble reliability and is also far below the minimum cluster counts (commonly cited as 25-50+, see item C3 evidence) below which even simpler statistical models are considered unreliable. XGBoost has no clustering-aware mechanism at all -- it will silently ignore the grouped structure and overfit to lake identity.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: needs-weak-labels, and worse than most items on this list: the target itself is typically a classical-method-derived proxy (see ground_truth_proxy_strategy), so this is arguably closer to 'the model is trained on possibly circular pseudo-labels with only 6 independent clusters' -- a compounding of two separate risks rather than one.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Not directly applicable -- XGBoost here operates on already-aggregated per-lake-year scalar features (areas, counts, rainfall totals), not on raw 20 m pixels, so there is no pretrained-resolution mismatch of the kind that affects image-based deep-learning items. The resolution question was already answered (or not) upstream, when the 20 m pixel counts were aggregated into the table's water/vegetation/built-up area columns.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: The project's own classical-method-derived area/fraction figures (MNDWI/NDVI thresholding), unless an independent target is substituted -- in which case the independence of that new target from the model's own input features must be re-checked.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None. It does not add rows (limitation 1 is the table's ceiling, and XGBoost cannot manufacture information that is not there), it does not make OSM building/road counts time-varying (limitation 2 -- see handles below, this is actively worse than neutral), it does nothing about the absence of ground truth (limitation 3), and it does not add within-year temporal resolution (limitation 4). If anything, running XGBoost on this table without disclosure risks manufacturing a false sense that limitation 1 has been addressed by 'using machine learning,' when the underlying data problem is unchanged.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No mechanism to. XGBoost sees whatever water-area feature is in the table and will fit to it exactly as given; it has no way to distinguish a drained-for-desilting year from an encroached year unless a separate feature explicitly flags desilting events (which would need to be manually researched and added per lake-year, effectively hand-coding the answer rather than the model discovering it). Bellandur's 15.7 -> 0.4 -> 107.9 ha swing would be fit by the trees as extreme, high-leverage data points from a single lake, most likely causing the model to build lake-identity-specific splits around Bellandur specifically -- reinforcing memorisation rather than generalisable pattern-finding.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No. If vegetation area/fraction is an input feature (as it likely is), it already conflates open water loss with hyacinth-mat gain exactly as the underlying classical method does; XGBoost inherits this conflation rather than resolving it, since it has no independent hyacinth signal unless one is engineered in from the MDPI Remote Sensing 2020 macrophyte mapping (doi 10.3390/rs12223843) as a new column -- again, hand-coding the answer rather than discovering it from 42 rows.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None beyond whatever the underlying table already encodes. XGBoost's output is a prediction/importance ranking over table columns that are themselves derived from the non-statutory OpenStreetMap lake polygon; it adds no independent connection to the Master Plan 30 m buffer, the quashed 75 m NGT buffer, KTCDA records, Survey of India records, Bhuvan, or the National Wetland Atlas 2024.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: This is the most concrete, checkable problem for this exact table, and the note is explicit about it: several features -- specifically ALL OpenStreetMap building and road counts, per project_constraints.building_data (a single 2026 OSM snapshot, 420,080 footprints) -- are constant within a lake across all 7 years. A feature that never changes within a group but differs strongly BETWEEN groups is mathematically indistinguishable, to a tree-splitting algorithm, from a lake-ID one-hot encoding: XGBoost will readily split on 'building_count > threshold_X' as a proxy for 'this row belongs to lake Y,' and any resulting SHAP importance attributed to building count is actually importance attributed to which lake it is, not to any real building-growth signal. This must be checked and disclosed for every feature in the table before modelling, exactly as the note instructs.

implementation.libraries: xgboost (Python package), shap (TreeExplainer), scikit-learn for cross-validation utilities and metrics, pandas for the tabular pipeline.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable. XGBoost is trained from scratch on the 42-row table every time; there is no meaningful pretrained-weights concept for gradient boosting on a bespoke tabular dataset.
implementation.licence: Fully open. xgboost is Apache 2.0 licensed, shap is MIT licensed. No licence blocker.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial to the point of irrelevance -- fitting XGBoost on 42 rows and a handful of features completes in well under a second on a laptop CPU; there is no compute constraint anywhere in this item. The constraint is entirely statistical, not computational.
implementation.student_days: 1-2 student-days to fit, tune (with heavy regularisation and shallow trees to fight overfitting), cross-validate with leave-one-lake-out, and generate SHAP plots -- the model itself is cheap to run. The larger, uncosted time sink is the honest write-up: explaining to a panel why a model that runs in milliseconds should not be trusted, and building the leave-one-lake-out and lake-identity-leakage diagnostics (checking which features are constant within-lake, re-running with those features removed, comparing SHAP rankings with and without lake ID as an explicit feature) realistically adds another 1-2 days on top of the modelling.

evaluation.metrics: If used at all: RMSE/MAE for a continuous target (e.g. predicted water-area change), or F1/AUC if reframed as a binary encroached/not-encroached classification -- but with only 6 independent clusters, none of these numbers should be reported as a single point estimate; a spread across leave-one-lake-out folds (6 numbers, one per held-out lake) is the only honest way to show what the metric actually looks like, and that spread is likely to be wide and unstable given 5 training lakes per fold.
evaluation.validation_protocol: leave-one-lake-out is the only defensible protocol, exactly as the field definition anticipates. Standard k-fold cross-validation on 42 rows drawn from only 6 clusters will place different years of the SAME lake into both train and test folds, letting the model see that lake's OSM building count, road count, and general water-area range during training and then 'predict' a held-out year of the same lake almost trivially -- this produces an artificially high and meaningless cross-validated score. With leave-one-lake-out, only 6 folds are possible, each training on just 5 lakes' worth of data (30 rows) and testing on a single unseen lake's 7 rows -- a genuinely hard generalisation task that most honestly reveals whether XGBoost has learned anything transferable at all.
evaluation.leakage_risk: This is the headline risk for the whole item. (1) Lake-identity leakage via constant features: as detailed above, OSM building/road counts are constant per lake and functionally encode lake ID, so any split that is not lake-based (or even a lake-based split, if these constant features are left in) allows the model to 'predict' by recognising which lake it is rather than by learning an encroachment relationship -- this alone can make an XGBoost model look impressively accurate while having learned nothing generalisable. (2) Target circularity: if the target is itself MNDWI/NDVI-derived, and vegetation/water-fraction features are also MNDWI/NDVI-derived, the model can partially predict the target from near-duplicate information, inflating apparent skill without any real explanatory content. (3) With only 6 clusters, even a correctly-specified leave-one-lake-out score has enormous variance -- a single unusual lake (Bellandur, with its desilting and hyacinth extremes) being the held-out fold can swing the reported metric dramatically in either direction, and 6 folds are nowhere near enough to average that noise out.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None by default -- XGBoost outputs a bare point prediction. Given 42 rows from 6 clusters and no ground truth, any reported metric or SHAP value without an accompanying interval is essentially unfalsifiable. Quantile regression objectives in XGBoost, or a conformal-prediction wrapper (item C7) calibrated via leave-one-lake-out residuals, are the minimum acceptable addition before any number from this model is shown to a panel -- and even then, with only 6 lakes, conformal coverage guarantees are themselves only approximately valid (see the conformal-prediction item's own caveats about very small n).
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: High risk if attempted, and should be flagged strongly. Given the 42-row ceiling, there is an obvious temptation to use SMOTE, a small tabular GAN, or simple interpolation to synthetically expand the lake-year table before fitting XGBoost or computing SHAP. Any such augmentation interpolates between only 6 real lakes' worth of examples and can easily fabricate a smooth, plausible-looking encroachment trend that is a pure artefact of the interpolation scheme rather than evidence of anything happening on the ground -- this is precisely the failure mode the project must avoid, since a panel cannot distinguish a genuine small-sample finding from an artificially smoothed one without seeing the raw 42 rows explicitly separated from any synthetic rows. If used at all, synthetic and real rows must be reported separately and never pooled into a single headline number.

evidence.published_performance: There is no dedicated published benchmark for 'XGBoost on a 42-row, 6-cluster lake-year table for encroachment prediction' -- this is a bespoke setup, not a named task with a leaderboard. General small-sample-size literature on gradient boosting (e.g. the G-XGBoost credit-risk work, Tandfonline 2021, doi 10.1080/08839514.2021.1987707) shows that XGBoost degrades gracefully compared to some alternatives on small tabular datasets and that generative augmentation can partially compensate [verify], but that literature addresses datasets of hundreds to low thousands of independent rows, not 42 rows drawn from only 6 clusters -- the clustering, not the raw row count, is this project's specific problem, and that specific problem is not addressed by the small-sample-XGBoost literature at all.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Generic small-sample XGBoost studies (e.g. credit risk, medical diagnosis accuracy curves) are drawn from tabular business or clinical datasets with independent observational units, not repeated-measures panel data with a handful of geographic clusters -- the analogy to this project's 6-lake, 7-year structure is weak at best.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No published instance of XGBoost with SHAP applied to Bengaluru or Indian urban lake encroachment tables was found. This would be a novel application, and the central finding worth reporting may well be a negative or null result about sample adequacy rather than a positive predictive result.
evidence.evidence_recency: 2021 for the closest generic small-sample XGBoost precedent (G-XGBoost); 2018-2020 for the TreeSHAP explainability method itself (Lundberg et al., NeurIPS 2017 original SHAP paper and the 2020 Nature Machine Intelligence TreeSHAP paper). The clustering/pseudoreplication problem this item's note foregrounds is better addressed by the mixed-model literature under item C3 than by anything specific to XGBoost.
evidence.primary_sources: Chen, T. & Guestrin, C. (2016), 'XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System', KDD 2016, https://doi.org/10.1145/2939672.2939785 ; Lundberg, S.M. et al. (2020), 'From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees', Nature Machine Intelligence 2:56-67, https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-019-0138-9 (the TreeSHAP paper) ; shap library documentation, https://shap.readthedocs.io/ ; G-XGBoost small-sample credit risk study, https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/08839514.2021.1987707 [verify exact reported accuracy figures] ; general caution on SHAP stability with small background data, arXiv:2204.11351, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.11351.

risk.failure_modes: (1) The model memorises lake identity through constant OSM building/road-count features rather than learning any real encroachment relationship -- this is close to guaranteed given the note's own observation that these features are constant within a lake. (2) With 6 clusters, leave-one-lake-out folds have such high variance that the reported metric is essentially noise -- a different random seed or minor hyperparameter change can flip which model 'looks better.' (3) SHAP values computed on 42 rows (or worse, on a single leave-one-lake-out test fold of just 7 rows) are themselves an average over so few observations that their confidence intervals, if computed honestly via bootstrap, would likely span from 'strongly positive' to 'strongly negative' contribution for the same feature -- the tidy, confident-looking SHAP beeswarm plot that panels find persuasive is not statistically supported at this n. (4) If the target is itself derived from the same MNDWI/NDVI pipeline as some input features, part of any reported predictive skill is circular by construction.
risk.panel_defensibility: This does not survive close questioning, and should be presented that way. The critical, hard-to-deflect question is: 'Building and road counts don't change over your 7 years -- so if XGBoost ranks them as important, isn't it just learning which lake it's looking at?' There is no good answer except 'yes, and we checked for this and removed/flagged it' -- if that check was not done, the entire SHAP-based interpretability story collapses under a single follow-up question. A second, equally hard question -- 'you have 6 lakes; how do you know this model generalises to a 7th?' -- has only one honest answer: it probably does not, and leave-one-lake-out cross-validation is offered as the best available (still weak) evidence either way. A panel with any statistical literacy will treat confident SHAP narratives built on 42 rows from 6 clusters as a red flag for overclaiming rather than a mark of rigour.
risk.honest_expectation: XGBoost will fit the 42-row table well in-sample (near-zero training error is easy at this row-to-parameter ratio) and will produce SHAP plots that look complete and professional, but its out-of-sample, leave-one-lake-out performance is realistically expected to be poor and highly variable, and a meaningful fraction of its apparent 'skill' and 'important features' will trace back to lake-identity memorisation via the constant OSM features rather than any discoverable encroachment signal. The honest, reportable finding is very likely to be a null or near-null result once lake-identity leakage is properly controlled for -- and reporting that null result, with the leakage diagnostic that produced it, is more valuable to the project than a polished but unsupported SHAP narrative.

verdict.recommended_rank: reject as a headline model; consider-with-reasons as a disclosed, heavily-caveated secondary exhibit -- 42 rows from 6 clusters cannot support gradient boosting as a genuine predictive claim, and the constant per-lake OSM features make lake-identity memorisation close to unavoidable; if shown at all, it should be shown specifically to demonstrate the leakage problem (e.g. SHAP importance collapsing to near-zero once lake ID and its proxies are removed), not as evidence of a working predictive model.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We tested XGBoost with SHAP on the 42-row lake-year table and found that, because several features are constant within each lake, the model was largely memorising which lake it was looking at rather than learning an encroachment relationship, so we are reporting this as a documented null result and diagnostic exercise rather than a predictive model, and treating the mixed-effects panel model as the statistically appropriate alternative.
